_read_this_first: See data/legal/README.md. This file is hand-written and human-reviewed. No code path in this application may write to it, and no language model may generate, extend, or 'improve' any field in it.
_policy: STATIC, HUMAN-REVIEWED DATASET. Overdose Good Samaritan immunity varies substantially between states and the statutes are amended frequently. A hallucinated legal protection is the single worst failure mode this product could have: it could persuade someone that calling for help is safe when it is not, or persuade them it is unsafe when protection exists. Summaries here are deliberately conservative and every record carries verified:false until a human has read the current statute.
_what_verified_false_means: verified:false is an HONEST DISCLOSURE, not an unfinished TODO. It means exactly this: the summary below was written conservatively by a human from general public-health understanding of how these laws work, and no human has yet sat down with the current statute text and confirmed it. The UI reads this flag and renders an 'unverified — confirm locally' banner beside the text. Shipping with the flag set true and no review done would be the dishonest option; shipping with it false and visible is the correct one.
_verification_required: Before any scored submission or public demo, a human must open the cited source for each state used, confirm the statute is current, correct the summary if needed, then set verified:true and fill in verified_by and verified_on. Do not flip the flag without doing the reading.
_deliberate_omissions: No record here states a quantity threshold, a penalty, a date of enactment, or a case citation. Those are the details that are easiest to state confidently and get wrong, and they change between legislative sessions. Where such a detail would matter, the record says to check it rather than guessing. The statute identifiers that appear in source_note fields are NAVIGATION POINTERS for the human reviewer — 'this is where to start looking' — not assertions that the cited section is current or says what the summary says.
_universal_guidance: In every jurisdiction, calling emergency services is the right thing to do. No US Good Samaritan law is a general shield against arrest, and none covers trafficking. Protection is typically conditional on calling in good faith, staying at the scene, and cooperating with responders. Nothing in this dataset is legal advice.

_field_guide.state_code: Two-letter USPS code. The key used by GET /api/legal/{state_code}.
_field_guide.has_immunity_law: Whether the state has some form of drug-overdose Good Samaritan protection. Set true only where that is broadly and publicly understood.
_field_guide.summary: Plain-language description of what calling 911 is generally understood to protect the caller and the overdosing person from.
_field_guide.does_not_cover: What the protection is generally understood NOT to reach. This field matters MORE than `summary`: overstating immunity is the dangerous error, understating it is the survivable one.
_field_guide.plain_language_line: One short sentence written to be read aloud to a frightened bystander who has seconds, not minutes. Calibrated to the strength of the protection — note that the Texas line is deliberately weaker than Kentucky's.
_field_guide.naloxone_note: Plain-language note on lay naloxone access in that state, where broadly understood. Empty where not confidently known.
_field_guide.verified: false until a human has read the current statute. See _what_verified_false_means.
_field_guide.verified_by: Name of the human reviewer. Empty until verified.
_field_guide.verified_on: ISO date of that review. Empty until verified.
_field_guide.source_note: What the human reviewer must confirm, and any state-specific warning about the shape of that state's law.
_field_guide.source_url: Official primary source to start from. Always a .gov or state legislature domain — never a secondary summary site.

states.summary: Kentucky has an overdose Good Samaritan law. In general terms, someone who in good faith seeks medical help for a suspected drug overdose, and who stays with the person until help arrives, has protection from prosecution for certain drug possession offences based on evidence obtained as a result of that call.
states.does_not_cover: Protection is generally limited to specified possession-type offences. It does not cover trafficking or distribution charges, outstanding warrants, or offences unrelated to the overdose. Whether parole or probation violations are covered must be confirmed against the current statute.
states.plain_language_line: In Kentucky, calling 911 for an overdose protects you. Call, and stay with them.
states.naloxone_note: Naloxone is broadly available from Kentucky pharmacies without an individual prescription, and lay administration is generally covered by separate protections. Confirm current access rules.
states.source_note: UNVERIFIED. Start at the KRS Chapter 218A controlled-substances provisions and locate the current overdose/emergency-assistance immunity section — KRS 218A.133 is the expected starting point, but confirm it is current and reads as summarised. Cross-check with the Kentucky Office of Drug Control Policy. This is the demo's default state, so verify this record first.

states.summary: Ohio has an overdose Good Samaritan law with conditions attached. In general terms it provides protection from prosecution for certain minor drug possession offences for a person who seeks medical assistance, subject to requirements that may include obtaining a screening and referral for treatment and limits on how many times the protection can be claimed.
states.does_not_cover: Conditional protection with usage limits and a follow-up requirement — one of the more qualified laws in the country. Does not cover trafficking offences, unrelated offences, or warrants. Whether it applies to someone under community control or parole must be confirmed.
states.plain_language_line: In Ohio, calling 911 for an overdose gives you legal protection. Call, and stay with them.
states.naloxone_note: Naloxone is broadly available in Ohio without an individual prescription. Confirm current access rules.
states.source_note: UNVERIFIED. Ohio attaches conditions that other states do not, so the does_not_cover field is the important one here. Start at the Ohio Revised Code Title 29 provisions on minor drug possession and overdose immunity — ORC 2925.11 is the expected starting point; confirm it is current. Cross-check with the Ohio Department of Health.

states.summary: West Virginia has an overdose Good Samaritan provision. In general terms, a person who in good faith seeks medical assistance for an overdose has protection from prosecution for certain low-level possession offences discovered as a result of the call, provided they remain at the scene and cooperate with responders.
states.does_not_cover: Not immunity from arrest generally. Does not extend to delivery or trafficking charges, to offences unrelated to the overdose, or to outstanding warrants. Conditions attach and have been amended more than once.
states.plain_language_line: In West Virginia, calling 911 for an overdose protects you. Call, and stay with them.
states.naloxone_note: Naloxone is broadly available to laypeople in West Virginia. Confirm current access rules.
states.source_note: UNVERIFIED. Start at the West Virginia Code, Chapter 16 public-health provisions and Chapter 60A controlled-substances provisions, and locate the current overdose-assistance immunity section. No section number is asserted here because this provision has been amended and renumbered; find it in the primary source.

states.summary: Pennsylvania has an overdose Good Samaritan law, commonly referenced alongside its statewide naloxone standing order. In general terms it protects both the caller and the overdosing person from prosecution for certain possession-level offences, where the caller reasonably believes an overdose is occurring, calls for help, gives their name to responders, and stays until help arrives.
states.does_not_cover: Does not cover delivery or trafficking. Does not clear unrelated charges, warrants, or supervision violations. The give-your-name-and-stay conditions are a genuine requirement rather than a formality, and protection can be lost by leaving the scene.
states.plain_language_line: In Pennsylvania, calling 911 for an overdose protects you — give your name and stay with them.
states.naloxone_note: Pennsylvania has operated a statewide standing order allowing laypeople to obtain naloxone from pharmacies. Confirm the order is still current.
states.source_note: UNVERIFIED. Start at the Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes, Title 35 health and safety provisions on drug overdose response immunity, and confirm the current text. Cross-check the naloxone standing order with the Pennsylvania Department of Health, since standing orders lapse and are reissued.

states.summary: New York has an overdose Good Samaritan law. In general terms, a person who in good faith seeks health care for someone experiencing a drug or alcohol overdose has protection from charges for certain controlled substance possession offences, paraphernalia offences, and some marijuana-related offences arising from that incident.
states.does_not_cover: Does not cover sale of a controlled substance above the thresholds set in the statute, and does not resolve unrelated charges or warrants. The quantity and offence-level boundaries are specific — read them in the statute rather than assuming them.
states.plain_language_line: In New York, calling 911 for an overdose protects you. Call, and stay with them.
states.naloxone_note: Naloxone is broadly available from New York pharmacies without an individual prescription, and community distribution programs operate statewide. Confirm current access rules.
states.source_note: UNVERIFIED. Start at the New York Penal Law provisions on medical-emergency-related immunity — Penal Law 220.78 is the expected starting point; confirm it is current and confirm the quantity thresholds rather than paraphrasing them. Cross-check with the NY State Department of Health opioid overdose prevention pages.

states.summary: California has an overdose Good Samaritan provision. In general terms, a person who in good faith seeks emergency medical assistance for someone experiencing a drug-related overdose has protection from arrest or prosecution for being under the influence, or for possessing a controlled substance or paraphernalia for personal use, where that evidence came from the emergency response.
states.does_not_cover: Does not extend to possession for sale, transportation, manufacture, distribution, or trafficking offences, and does not clear unrelated warrants. Does not apply where the call is not made in good faith.
states.plain_language_line: In California, calling 911 for an overdose protects you. Call, and stay with them.
states.naloxone_note: Naloxone is broadly available to laypeople in California through pharmacies and community distribution programs. Confirm current access rules.
states.source_note: UNVERIFIED. Start at the California Health and Safety Code, Division 10 controlled-substances provisions on overdose-related immunity — section 11376.5 is the expected starting point; confirm it is current. Cross-check with California Department of Public Health naloxone pages.

states.summary: Florida has an overdose Good Samaritan provision within its drug overdose prevention law. In general terms, a person acting in good faith who seeks medical assistance for someone experiencing a drug-related overdose has protection from prosecution for certain possession offences arising from evidence obtained as a result.
states.does_not_cover: Does not extend to sale, trafficking, manufacture, or distribution offences, and does not clear unrelated warrants or supervision violations. Protection is tied to the emergency response and to acting in good faith.
states.plain_language_line: In Florida, calling 911 for an overdose protects you. Call, and stay with them.
states.naloxone_note: Naloxone is available to laypeople in Florida through pharmacies and community programs. Confirm current access rules.
states.source_note: UNVERIFIED. Start at the Florida Statutes Chapter 893 drug-abuse-prevention provisions on overdose-related immunity — section 893.21 is the expected starting point; confirm it is current. Cross-check with Florida Department of Health naloxone pages.

states.summary: Texas has a limited overdose Good Samaritan defence, enacted later than most states and materially narrower. In general terms it provides a defence to prosecution for certain small-quantity possession offences for a person who calls for emergency medical help, remains at the scene, and cooperates — but eligibility restrictions apply that do not exist elsewhere.
states.does_not_cover: One of the narrowest such laws in the country. Exclusions may include limits based on the caller's prior record and on whether someone else had already called for help. Does not cover trafficking or larger quantities, unrelated offences, or warrants. Do not describe Texas protection to a bystander as though it were as broad as Kentucky's or New York's.
states.plain_language_line: In Texas, there is some legal protection for calling 911 during an overdose, and calling is still the right thing to do.
states.naloxone_note: Naloxone is available to laypeople in Texas under a standing order. Confirm current access rules.
states.source_note: UNVERIFIED, and the highest-risk record in this file. Start at the Texas Health and Safety Code provisions establishing a defence to prosecution for overdose-related possession. Read the EXCLUSIONS in full before this record is shown to anyone — in Texas the exclusions matter more than the protection, which is why plain_language_line is deliberately hedged.

_fallback.summary: We do not have a reviewed entry for this state, so we are not going to guess. Most US states have some form of Good Samaritan overdose law, but the protections differ and we will not describe one we have not checked.
_fallback.does_not_cover: Assume nothing about immunity here. No US Good Samaritan law is a general shield against arrest, and none of them covers trafficking charges.
_fallback.plain_language_line: Calling 911 is still the right thing to do. Call, and stay with them.
_fallback.source_note: No reviewed entry. Served by GET /api/legal/{state_code} when the requested state is not in `states`. Refusing to answer is the correct behaviour: a plausible-sounding invented summary is the exact failure mode this entire file exists to prevent.
